chunks.text: A solid can be viewed as a stack of thin slabs, each a cross section with some area extended through a small thickness.
The volume of one slab is the cross-sectional area times the thickness, A(x)·dx.
The volume of a solid with known cross sections is V = ∫ from a to b of A(x) dx.
The formula works for any solid as long as the cross-sectional area can be written as a function of position.
Finding A(x) requires the shape of the cross section (given) and its size (read from the base region).
For slices perpendicular to the x-axis, the key length at position x is the height of the base, top − bottom = f(x) − g(x).
This key length is the side of a square, the base of a triangle, or the diameter of a semicircle, depending on the stated shape.
A square cross section of side s has area s².
An equilateral triangle of side s has area (√3/4)s².
A semicircle of diameter s has radius s/2 and area (1/2)π(s/2)² = πs²/8.
A semicircle of radius s has area (1/2)πs², used only when s is the radius rather than the diameter.
For a semicircle, the base length is usually the diameter, so the radius is half of it; treating s as the radius quadruples the area.
Example: a base under y = √x from 0 to 4 with square cross sections has side √x, area x, and volume ∫₀⁴ x dx = 8.
For cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis, the slabs stack along x and you integrate V = ∫ A(x) dx.
For cross sections perpendicular to the y-axis, the slabs stack along y, the length is right − left, and you integrate V = ∫ A(y) dy.
The phrase 'cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis (or y-axis)' tells you which variable to integrate with respect to.
Example: with base between y = x and y = x², the length is s = x − x², and semicircular cross sections give volume π/240.
The same base with equilateral-triangle cross sections gives volume √3/120, differing only by the area formula.
The volume formula is a Riemann sum of slab volumes A(xᵢ)·Δx that converges to ∫ A(x) dx as the slabs get thinner.
Common errors are using a function value instead of top − bottom, using the wrong shape area formula, and confusing a semicircle's diameter with its radius.
The cross-section method generalizes to volumes of revolution, where the cross sections are circles (discs) or rings (washers).
The unifying technique of the integration unit is to slice an accumulated quantity into measurable pieces, write the measure of a generic piece, and integrate.
